gaps.sentence: My laptop, ___ I bought only last year, has already crashed twice.
gaps.explanation: Non-defining clause about a thing: 'which', never 'that'.

gaps.sentence: The film, ___ was shot entirely in Iceland, won three awards.
gaps.explanation: After a comma, 'that' is impossible: use 'which'.

gaps.sentence: Our new neighbours, ___ have three children, moved in last week.
gaps.hint: people as subject; clause between commas
gaps.explanation: 'Who' is used for people in non-defining clauses; 'which' is for things.

gaps.sentence: She was two hours late, ___ annoyed the interviewer.
gaps.hint: comment on the whole situation before the comma
gaps.explanation: When a clause comments on the whole previous statement, use 'which' after the comma.

gaps.sentence: That's the boy ___ dog won first prize at the show.
gaps.hint: the dog belongs to the boy
gaps.explanation: 'Whose dog' means 'his dog'; 'who's' would mean 'who is', which makes no sense here.

gaps.sentence: The moment ___ she saw the results, she burst into tears.
gaps.explanation: 'When' links the moment to the action; 'where' and 'why' do not fit a time noun.

gaps.sentence: Mount Everest, ___ was first climbed in 1953, attracts hundreds of climbers every year.
gaps.explanation: 'Which' introduces extra information about the mountain; 'that' is wrong after a comma.

gaps.sentence: It is one of the most impressive buildings ___ I have ever seen.
gaps.explanation: After superlative expressions, 'that' is the standard relative pronoun in defining clauses.
